mcqs.question: A responsive layout is verified at 375px and 768px and looks correct at both. What is the most likely remaining gap?
options: Intermediate and landscape widths: breakpoints are snapshots, and fluid sizing must hold at every width between them
Nothing significant: if the two most common device classes pass, the layout is validated
Only widths above the largest breakpoint, since the 375px check already covers all narrow screens
Orientation does not need testing because media queries handle it automatically
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the guidance is to validate at narrow, wide, and intermediate widths, because a layout that works only at two breakpoint snapshots can still fail between them, which is exactly where landscape phones sit. The strongest distractor is option 2: device-class snapshot testing feels thorough but says nothing about the continuum of widths and orientations between and beyond the two checked points.

mcqs.question: You build a horizontal drag carousel on mobile web. During a drag the browser sometimes takes over and starts scrolling vertically instead. What is the correct fix?
options: Declare touch-action on the drag region (for example none, or pan-y if vertical scroll should remain) so the browser knows which gestures the region owns
Call event.preventDefault() inside every pointermove handler to cancel the scrolling
Attach non-passive touchstart listeners and cancel all touch events globally on the page
Filter handlers to pointerType === 'touch' only and ignore mouse and pen events
mcqs.explanation: Correct: with Pointer Events, the browser decides whether it may pan or zoom from the region's touch-action property, so you declare what the region owns instead of cancelling everything globally (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Pointer_events). The strongest distractor is option 2: preventDefault inside a pointer handler does not control browser panning, which is why the takeover keeps happening despite the cancellation attempts.

mcqs.question: During a Pointer Events drag, the pointer moves fast and leaves the element's bounds; pointermove events stop arriving at the original target. What keeps the drag alive?
options: setPointerCapture(event.pointerId) on the element at drag start, so subsequent events stay targeted to it even outside its bounds
Attaching a pointermove listener to document and manually hit-testing every move
Setting touch-action: none on the entire page
Calling event.stopPropagation() in the pointerdown handler
mcqs.explanation: Correct: pointer capture keeps subsequent events targeted to the capturing element even if the pointer leaves it, and it should be released on completion or cancellation. The strongest distractor is option 2: a document-level listener with manual hit-testing reimplements capture badly, because it still needs capture semantics to survive fast moves and to receive the events that matter during the drag.

mcqs.question: Which set correctly names the current Core Web Vitals and their recommended good thresholds?
options: LCP within 2.5 seconds, INP at or below 200 milliseconds, CLS at or below 0.1
FCP within 1.8 seconds, FID at or below 100 milliseconds, CLS at or below 0.1
LCP within 2.5 seconds, TTI within 3.8 seconds, CLS at or below 0.1
LCP within 1.2 seconds, INP at or below 200 milliseconds, CLS at or below 0.25
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the current Core Web Vitals are LCP for loading (2.5s), INP for interactivity (200ms), and CLS for visual stability (0.1), evaluated at the 75th percentile (web.dev: https://web.dev/articles/vitals). The strongest distractor is option 2: FCP and FID are real metrics and FID was the predecessor interactivity metric, but neither is part of the current Core Web Vitals set.

mcqs.question: Field data shows an INP regression on mobile but not on desktop, and you cannot reproduce it on your development machine. What is the correct next step?
options: Segment the field data by mobile device and route, use lab tooling to reproduce the likely cause, ship a fix, and confirm in field data again
Close the investigation: a performance issue that cannot be reproduced locally is not real
Apply every optimization available: memoize all components and defer all scripts, then watch the metric
Report only the desktop score, since that is what most stakeholders use
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the workflow is to segment field data by mobile device and page or route, reproduce the likely cause with lab tooling, ship an experiment, and compare field data after rollout, keeping real-user monitoring because lab results are not a substitute for field measurement. The strongest distractor is option 3: shotgun optimization changes many variables at once, so even if the metric moves you learn nothing about the cause, and it risks new regressions.

mcqs.question: Product asks for the offline banner copy: Your changes will sync automatically within 5 minutes of reconnecting. What is the most accurate engineering response?
options: We can queue writes and retry them, but we cannot promise a time: Background Sync retries are limited, service workers can be stopped, and periodic sync is browser-controlled
Yes: Background Sync guarantees delivery once the network returns
Yes, if we set a timer in the service worker with setInterval
No, nothing can ever run in the background on the web
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Background Sync can retry short work but browsers limit retries and execution time, service workers can be stopped, and periodic background sync is browser-controlled rather than a guaranteed schedule, so the UI must never promise that a background task will definitely run at a particular time (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Progressive_web_apps/Guides/Offline_and_background_operation). The strongest distractor is option 2: it converts a best-effort retry mechanism into a delivery guarantee the platform does not offer.

mcqs.question: Stakeholders want the same one-tap install prompt flow on iPhone that Chrome shows on Android. What is accurate?
options: On iOS and iPadOS there is no browser install prompt; users add the app manually through the browser share menu, so the flow must be platform-aware
Safari fires the same install prompt event as Chrome, so the flow can be reused
iOS supports install prompts only for apps with a paid Apple Developer account
iOS PWAs cannot be installed at all
mcqs.explanation: Correct: on iOS and iPadOS there is no browser install prompt and users add the app manually through the share menu, with display modes and capabilities that differ from desktop and Android, so installation should be productized as progressive enhancement with a platform-specific path (web.dev: https://web.dev/learn/pwa/installation). The strongest distractor is option 2: it assumes install UX is a uniform web capability, which is precisely the misconception that produces broken iOS funnels.

scenarios.prompt: This drag handle works with a mouse on desktop but misbehaves on touch: the browser sometimes scrolls instead of dragging, fast drags lose the element, and after a failed drag the handle stays stuck until the next tap. Find the bugs and rewrite the interaction.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Three defects, all touch-specific. First, gesture ownership: the code never declares touch-action, so on touch the browser is free to take over the drag for its own panning, which is why the page scrolls instead. preventDefault inside the pointer handlers does not control browser panning; the fix is a CSS declaration on the handle, touch-action: none for a pure drag, or pan-y if vertical page scrolling should survive while horizontal drags are custom. Second, event targeting: without pointer capture, a fast drag leaves the handle's bounds and pointermove retargets to whatever element the pointer is over, so the drag dies mid-gesture. Call handle.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId) in pointerdown and release it in the cleanup paths. Third, the missing end state: when the browser reclaims the gesture it fires pointercancel, not pointerup, so the move listener is never removed and the handle appears stuck. Handle pointercancel exactly like pointerup: remove the listener, release capture, and reset visual state. A corrected version: in pointerdown, setPointerCapture and attach move; in a shared end() function used by both pointerup and pointercancel, remove the listener and release capture if held. Keep move handlers small and only update the visual state that must change. Finally, a drag is a spatial gesture, so pair it with a semantic alternative (buttons or a slider) so the action is not gesture-only, and test with mouse, pen, and touch rather than pointerType checks unless device-specific behavior is genuinely needed.
rubric: Identifies touch-action as the mechanism that declares which browser gestures the region owns, and knows preventDefault in pointer handlers does not stop panning
Uses setPointerCapture on pointerdown and releases it on completion, explaining why fast drags otherwise lose the target
Treats pointercancel as a required end state alongside pointerup, and explains that the browser reclaiming the gesture is what fires it
Keeps move handling minimal and mentions a keyboard or semantic alternative for the action
Tests across mouse, pen, and touch instead of filtering on pointerType without cause

scenarios.prompt: Review this service worker for a PWA that must show reasonably fresh data and safely sync user edits made offline. What does it get wrong, and how should the offline behavior be designed instead?
scenarios.modelAnswer: The fetch handler applies cache-first to every API request. Cache-first favors speed but serves potentially stale assets, so API data cached once is replayed indefinitely: users see old data even when online, with no freshness signal and no fallback policy. The fix is a per-resource strategy: network-first for API data, falling back to the cache when the network fails, and cache-first only where staleness is acceptable, such as versioned static assets. The UI should also expose freshness, so cached responses are presented as what they are. The sync handler has the more dangerous bugs. First, replay is not idempotent: if a POST reaches the server but the response is lost, or the sync is retried, the same edit is applied twice. Each queued operation needs an idempotency mechanism so replaying it cannot duplicate the side effect. Second, there is no conflict policy: the server may have newer state from another device, and the code has no defined outcome for that collision; conflict resolution must be decided before queued mutations are enabled. Third, the loop is all-or-nothing: one failed fetch rejects the waitUntil, the remaining operations never run, and because browsers limit Background Sync retries and execution time, and the service worker can be stopped between attempts, the queue can strand. Each operation should be attempted and persisted independently, with per-op error handling. Finally, the product copy around this must never promise that a background task will run at a particular time: periodic sync is browser-controlled, retries are limited, and the UI must tolerate failure while showing what is saved locally and what is pending sync.
rubric: Rejects cache-first for API data and chooses a per-resource strategy, network-first for freshness with cache fallback
Identifies non-idempotent replay as the critical safety bug and requires idempotent writes
Requires a defined conflict resolution policy before queued mutations are enabled
Makes the sync loop per-operation and tolerant of partial failure instead of all-or-nothing
Refuses to promise background execution timing in the UI and exposes pending-sync state

scenarios.prompt: At 600px in landscape the cards overflow horizontally; at 320px they almost fit but the text is cramped; between 780px and 1000px the row is mostly empty space. Redesign the responsive approach and describe how you would validate it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The root problem is device-snapshot thinking: one fixed card width (480px) plus one breakpoint at a single phone width (375px), so every width that is not exactly those two points gets a compromised layout. The redesign starts from content and fluid sizing: replace the fixed card width with flexible tracks, for example a grid with auto-fill and minmax so the column count adapts continuously to the available space, or flexbox with percentage-based cards that wrap. Make the images responsive so they scale with their container instead of carrying a fixed 960px width, and keep text readable at the smallest widths rather than merely fitting. If this card is reused in contexts with different available widths (page grid versus sidebar), give the component its own breakpoint with a container query instead of inheriting the page's device media queries. Validation is where the original approach failed: test at narrow, wide, and intermediate widths, in portrait and landscape, with real content (long names, missing images), not just the two popular device widths; a layout that works at two snapshots can still fail between them. Treat touch targets and readability as requirements of the mobile pass, and measure real mobile users separately in field data, since the Core Web Vitals guidance recommends segmenting results by mobile and desktop rather than reading one aggregate.
rubric: Replaces fixed pixel card widths with fluid sizing and flexible layout primitives (grid or flexbox)
Makes images responsive rather than fixed-size, and keeps text readable at the smallest widths
Reaches for container queries when the component, not the page, needs its own breakpoint
Validates at narrow, wide, and intermediate widths in both orientations with real content, not two device snapshots
Segments performance field data by mobile instead of relying on an aggregate score
